items.title: The Design Space of Tri-Modal Masked Diffusion Models
items.abstract: Discrete diffusion models have emerged as strong alternatives to autoregressive language models, with recent work initializing and finetuning a base unimodal model for bi-modal generation. Diverging from previous approaches, we introduce the first tri-modal Masked Diffusion Models (MDM) pretrained from scratch on text, image-text, and audio-text data. We systematically analyze multimodal scaling laws, modality mixing ratios, noise schedules, batch-size effects and provide optimized inference sampling defaults. Our batch-size analysis yields a novel stochastic differential equation (SDE) based…
items.title_ko: Apple, 텍스트·이미지·오디오 통합 Tri-Modal Masked Diffusion Model 처음부터 사전학습
items.summary: 이 블로그는 텍스트, 이미지-텍스트, 오디오-텍스트 데이터를 처음부터 함께 사전학습한 **최초의 삼중 모달(tri-modal) Masked Diffusion Model(MDM)**을 소개한다. 기존 연구가 단일 모달 기반 모델을 초기화·파인튜닝해 이중 모달 생성을 구현한 것과 달리, 이 연구는 세 모달리티를 동시에 다룬다. 멀티모달 스케일링 법칙, 모달리티 혼합 비율, 노이즈 스케줄, 배치 크기 효과를 체계적으로 분석하고 최적화된 추론 샘플링 기본값을 제시한다. 배치 크기 분석에서는 새로운 확률미분방정식(SDE) 기반 접근을 도출했다.
items.why_it_matters: 텍스트·이미지·오디오를 아우르는 통합 생성 모델의 설계 지침(스케일링 법칙, 모달 혼합 비율 등)을 체계적으로 제공해, 향후 멀티모달 확산 모델 개발 시 참고할 수 있는 실증적 근거를 마련한다.
items.whats_different: 기존 연구는 단일 모달로 사전학습된 모델을 초기화해 이중 모달로 파인튜닝하는 방식이었으나, 이 연구는 **세 가지 모달리티를 처음부터 함께 사전학습**한다는 점에서 다르다.

items.title: Google DeepMind and Singapore Government collaborate to build fine-tuned AI model for scam detection
items.abstract: Learn how Google DeepMind and GovTech Singapore uses lightweight on-device Gemma models to intercept conversational scams in private chats with zero cloud data egress.
items.title_ko: DeepMind·싱가포르 정부, 온디바이스 Gemma로 대화형 스캠 실시간 차단 — 클라우드 데이터 유출 無
items.summary: Google DeepMind와 GovTech Singapore가 협력해 경량 Gemma 모델을 온디바이스에서 구동, 개인 채팅 내 대화형 스캠을 실시간으로 탐지한다. 모델이 기기 내에서 직접 추론을 수행하기 때문에 **클라우드로 데이터가 전송되지 않는다**. 메시지 내용이 외부 서버로 나가지 않으면서도 사기성 대화 패턴을 식별할 수 있다는 점이 핵심이다.
items.why_it_matters: 개인정보가 민감한 메신저 환경에서 **온디바이스 AI**로 보안 기능을 구현한 정부-빅테크 협업 사례로, 프라이버시와 보안을 동시에 만족시키려는 실용적 접근을 보여준다.
items.whats_different: 클라우드 기반 스캠 탐지 서비스와 달리 대화 데이터를 서버로 전송하지 않고 기기 내에서 처리한다는 점이 다르다.

In multistage engineering workflows, an undetected error early in setup can silently propagate through downstream stages and final artifact generation. items.title_ko: NVIDIA, NeMo Gym으로 칩 설계용 AI 에이전트 신뢰성·툴콜 효율 개선
items.summary: 칩 설계처럼 다단계 엔지니어링 워크플로우에서는 AI 에이전트가 그럴듯하지만 틀린 산출물을 생성해도 초기 단계의 오류가 감지되지 않은 채 후속 단계와 최종 산출물로 조용히 전파될 수 있다. 이는 AI 에이전트의 실제 프로덕션 도입을 가로막는 주요 신뢰성 문제로 지적된다. NVIDIA는 **NeMo Gym**을 활용해 이러한 에이전트를 평가하고 개선하는 방법을 소개한다.
items.why_it_matters: 에이전트 생성 오류가 다단계 워크플로우에서 눈에 띄지 않고 누적되는 문제는 칩 설계 외에도 복잡한 엔지니어링 자동화 전반에 적용되는 중요한 신뢰성 리스크다.

items.title: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
items.abstract: Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speech…
items.title_ko: Apple, 음성 기반 모델의 '언어 선택적 차원'으로 전사 없이 코드스위칭 직접 탐지
items.summary: 코드스위칭(CS)은 한 발화 내에서 언어가 번갈아 나타나는 현상으로 다국어 음성에서 흔하지만 사전학습 데이터에는 충분히 반영되지 않는다. 기존 방식은 음성을 전사한 뒤 텍스트에서 언어 전환을 탐지하는데, 이는 정확한 다국어 전사 결과에 의존한다는 한계가 있다. 이 연구는 사전학습된 음성 기반 모델 내부의 프레임 단위 언어 정보를 활용해 **전사 과정 없이** 음성에서 직접 CS를 탐지하는 경량 방법을 제안한다.
items.why_it_matters: 다국어 음성 코퍼스에서 CS 발화를 효율적으로 찾아낼 수 있으면 사전학습 데이터의 언어 다양성을 늘릴 수 있어, 다국어·코드스위칭 음성 인식 성능 개선에 기여할 수 있다.
items.whats_different: 음성을 텍스트로 전사한 후 언어 전환을 탐지하던 **기존 전사 기반 방식**과 달리, 음성 모델 내부의 언어 선택적 차원을 활용해 전사 단계 없이 직접 탐지한다.

items.title: Measuring the Impact of Personalized Recommendations
items.abstract: By Kevin Zielnicki, Guy Aridor, Aurélien Bibaut, Allen Tran, Winston Chou, and Nathan Kallus Introduction Personalization is everywhere on the internet. It shapes the products we discover, the stories we read, the music we hear, and the movies and TV shows we watch. At Netflix, personalization has been central to the member experience for decades — from the Netflix Prize to our modern recommender system that helps members navigate a large and constantly changing catalog. But personalization is not only an algorithmic problem, it is also a measurement problem. How do we know how much value personalization creates? More precisely, how do we separate the appeal of a title from the value created by recommending that title to the right member at the right time? In a new article in the International Journal of Industrial Organization — which we are also presenting at this year’s ACM Conference on Economics & Computation (EC ‘26) — we develop a model of member behavior, title choice, and personalized recommendations. The model lets us estimate how recommendations affect both whether members choose to watch and, if so, which titles they choose. In this post, we summarize our approach and main findings. The Measurement Challenge A natural first attempt at valuing recommendations is to ask: what share of viewing comes from titles that were recommended? This is an intuitive metric, but it fails to answer the causal question at hand. The problem is that recommendations are not randomly assigned. A title appears on a member’s homepage precisely because the recommender system predicts that the member might want to watch it. If a member watches that title, was it because the recommendation caused the member to watch it? Or would she have watched it anyway because of her underlying preference for that kind of title? This is the core measurement challenge: recommendations are targeted to demand, so viewing a recommended title combines the effect of personalization with the member’s underlying preferences. One way to solve this would be to run a large experiment that replaces Netflix’s personalized experience with an unpersonalized one. That would create clean variation — but it would also be a poor member experience. Personalization is a central part of how members locate valuable titles in a large catalog, so turning it off broadly is not an acceptable measurement strategy. Instead, we take a hybrid approach. We build a behavioral model that separates members’ underlying preferences from the incremental effect of recommendations. The model uses the natural variation in the recommendation system, for example due to algorithmic exploration, to estimate how recommendations affect choice. Then, to validate the model predictions about title substitutability, we use small-scale A/B tests that “nudge” the salience of a handful of titles exogenously, generating ground-truth substitution patterns for a subset of titles. This lets us combine the scale and richness of modeling with the credibility of experimental evidence. A Model of Member Choice To measure the value of personalization, we need a model of what members would watch under different recommendation systems. Our model treats Netflix viewing as a day-by-day choice process. On each day, a member chooses among the titles available in the catalog, or she chooses not to watch anything. This gives us a concrete target to estimate: the probability that a member watches each title on a given day, as a function of their preferences, their viewing history, and the recommendations they see. A simple version of this model would be too restrictive. It might assume, for example, that removing one title from the catalog shifts viewing toward all other titles in roughly proportional ways. But that isn’t how member choice works. If a member is considering a romantic comedy, the closest substitutes are likely other romantic comedies, not every title on Netflix equally. items.title_ko: Netflix, 개인화 추천의 인과적 가치 측정 모델 공개 — 알고리즘 탐색 변동과 A/B 테스트 결합 검증
items.summary: Netflix가 개인화 추천이 시청에 미치는 실제 효과를 측정하는 행동 모델을 개발해 International Journal of Industrial Organization에 발표하고 ACM EC '26에서도 공개한다. 핵심 문제는 추천이 무작위로 노출되지 않고 이미 수요가 예측된 제목에 집중되므로, 추천된 제목의 시청이 추천 효과 때문인지 원래 선호 때문인지 구분하기 어렵다는 점이다. 이를 풀기 위해 전체 개인화를 끄는 실험 대신, **알고리즘 탐색에서 발생하는 자연적 변동**을 활용해 회원의 선택 확률을 추정하는 모델을 구축했다. 모델의 제목 대체 가능성 예측은 소규모 A/B 테스트로 일부 제목의 노출도를 외생적으로 조정해 얻은 실측 대체 패턴과 비교해 검증했다.
items.why_it_matters: 대규모 개인화 시스템을 전면 중단하지 않고도 그 인과적 가치를 측정할 방법을 제시한다는 점에서, 추천 시스템 운영 조직이 겪는 '측정은 하고 싶지만 실험은 할 수 없는' 딜레마에 대한 실무적 해법을 보여준다.
items.whats_different: 모든 제목으로 시청이 균등하게 대체된다고 가정하는 단순 모델과 달리, 로맨틱 코미디처럼 **유사 장르 내 대체**를 반영하는 구조를 사용하고, 이를 전면적 무작위 실험이 아닌 기존 추천 시스템의 알고리즘 탐색 변동과 소규모 A/B 테스트 조합으로 검증한다.

items.title: DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack
items.abstract: by Olek Gorajek , Samuel Redai , Yian Shang Intro Our Netflix journey from data to dashboards, particularly within the space of the experimentation platform, always presented a unique set of challenges. This blog post aims to illuminate these hurdles and explain how an innovative open-source metric platform became instrumental in overcoming some of them. We’ll showcase the critical role that DataJunction played in streamlining our data workflows and enhancing our ability to derive meaningful insights from our vast datasets. Metrics are the foundation of data-driven decision-making, but at many organizations, they are scattered, inconsistently defined, and difficult to discover or trust. At Netflix, this challenge first became apparent in our experimentation platform, where reliable metrics are essential for interpreting test results. But the complexity of the original tooling made it very difficult to understand and introspect these metrics both in terms of their definitions as well as their values. Initial Problem Scattered metric definitions, redundant datasets, and pipelines are often a natural effect of a fast-moving company with a large and powerful analytical workforce. This is a common problem in big data-driven firms, and it is not easy to solve across multiple departments, which are often governed by somewhat different rules and regulations. An easy-to-use, well-governed, and centralized semantic layer can help with these issues. Our initial problem was most evident in our Experimentation Platform team, where the previous system required: extensive business knowledge familiarity with experimentation conventions and complex engineering practices This led to metric authoring processes that would take weeks, which was a prohibitive requirement for Data Scientists and Analytics Engineers who wanted to onboard new metrics to the Experimentation Platform. Enter DataJunction To address this problem and to set ourselves on the path to a successful semantic layer solution in the future, we looked at several candidates. Among other solutions we evaluated Mando (an internal framework), Minerva (an open source semantic layer from AirBnB), and DataJunction (another open source solution, “DJ” for short). All of them had some strength, but DJ offered one thing that the others did not at the time: a solid SQL parsing and SQL generation engine. At the time of the POC, DJ was also the only open-source solution that stored all its definitions in a connected graph, similar to how relational databases store metadata on their views and queries. Easy “SQL wrangling” with rich metadata was the main feature that convinced us to try it for our immediate use case. DataJunction originated from a similar internal Facebook project created (around 2015) by the data science and infrastructure (DSI) team, mainly as an answer to the need for metrics portability. During several iterations of the Deltoid project — which was the main experimentation platform at Facebook at the time — users were required to rebuild and repopulate their metrics when they wanted to move to the next version of Deltoid. But after implementing DJ and abstracting all metric definitions the team offered seamless migrations by separating the concerns between the metrics and the stats computation platform. That project was subsequently renamed to MDF (Metrics and Dimensions Factory) and promoted as a generic semantic layer used widely by various departments. In 2021, one of the Facebook engineers ( Beto Dealmeida ), started the DJ Github project and built out some basic functionality. Then together with some folks at Netflix expanded the scope further, and soon after that the project was introduced at Netflix. Following that introduction, three Netflix engineers (authors of this blog) together with a couple of external contributors, most notably Nick Ouellet , have been building out the remaining features of the platform. items.title_ko: Netflix, 오픈소스 시맨틱 레이어 DataJunction으로 실험 플랫폼 메트릭 정의 주 단위 소요를 해결
items.summary: Netflix 실험 플랫폼은 메트릭 정의가 흩어져 있고 일관성이 없어 신뢰하기 어려운 문제를 겪었으며, 기존 도구는 복잡한 엔지니어링 지식을 요구해 메트릭 등록에 **몇 주가 소요**되는 구조였다. 이를 해결하기 위해 Mando, Minerva, DataJunction(DJ) 세 후보를 검토했고, 강력한 SQL 파싱·생성 엔진과 그래프 기반 정의 저장 구조를 갖춘 DJ를 채택했다. DJ는 원래 2015년경 Facebook DSI 팀의 내부 프로젝트에서 출발해 실험 플랫폼 Deltoid의 메트릭 이식성 문제를 해결하며 MDF로 발전했고, 2021년 Beto Dealmeida가 오픈소스 Github 프로젝트로 시작했다. 이후 Netflix 엔지니어 3명과 외부 기여자들이 플랫폼의 나머지 기능을 함께 구축해왔다.
items.why_it_matters: 조직 전반에 흩어진 메트릭 정의를 중앙화하는 시맨틱 레이어는 데이터 기반 의사결정의 신뢰성과 속도를 좌우하는 공통 과제이며, 대규모 데이터 조직이라면 유사한 메트릭 거버넌스 문제를 겪을 가능성이 높다.
items.whats_different: 기존 내부 솔루션 Mando나 오픈소스 Minerva와 달리, DJ는 관계형 데이터베이스가 뷰·쿼리 메타데이터를 저장하는 방식과 유사하게 모든 정의를 **연결된 그래프**로 저장하는 유일한 오픈소스 솔루션이었다는 점이 채택 결정 요인이었다.

items.title: Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs
items.abstract: Authors: Nick Rutigliano , Argha C , Samartha Chandrashekar How we detect failing GPUs and network fabric, remediate machines automatically, and let long-running jobs survive hardware loss. Open Netflix, and the home screen is assembled for you: which rows appear, the order they appear in, the titles within them, and the artwork for each title are chosen by machine learning models trained on how hundreds of millions of members watch. Personalization is one of the most widely used things we build, and members feel it every time they open the app. Like a growing share of Netflix, it runs on GPUs, which train those models and increasingly serve them live. Those GPUs have to stay healthy for that experience to hold up, and keeping them healthy is harder than it sounds. A single large training job can run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs spread over many machines. It runs as a gang: the ranks move in lockstep, exchanging data every step, so the job advances only as fast as its slowest participant and stops entirely if one participant dies. Every GPU, every high-speed network adapter, and every interconnect must keep working throughout the run. At the scale at which modern machine learning runs, individual GPUs and network links can fail during a run, so the underlying platform must be prepared for this and handle it without a person in the loop. This post describes how we keep our GPU infrastructure healthy for training and inference. We cover how we detect failing hardware before and during jobs, how we automatically remediate a bad machine, and how we let a long job survive the loss of a machine. These training workloads run on our modern Kubernetes-native Compute platform. Why GPU reliability matters Netflix aims to entertain the world, and machine learning has been part of how we do that for years, from the recommendations that help members find something to watch to the systems that help produce and promote titles. As generative AI advances, we are investing in it on both sides of the business: for members, through better recommendations and higher-quality promotional assets; and for storytelling, through creative tools for our production partners. All of this runs on GPUs, for both training and inference, and GPU capacity is among the fastest-growing and most expensive parts of our infrastructure. That makes reliability a business concern on two fronts. — - Availability: a training run that loses a machine, or an inference service that cannot get healthy capacity, delays work that members and creators depend on. Cost efficiency: a GPU sitting idle behind a slow neighbor, or a whole machine pulled from the pool because one device is degraded, becomes capacity we paid for and are not using. Higher reliability and higher utilization mean more useful work per GPU, which is equivalent to spending less to do the same work. Inference is a growing share of that GPU footprint as more of these AI features reach members, so the reliability and efficiency that matter for multi-week training runs increasingly matter for always-on serving too. Why basic health checks are not enough We start from the baseline provided by the cloud provider. Cloud providers run instance status checks on virtual machines: a system status check for the underlying host’s power, network, and hardware reachability; an instance status check to verify that the operating system is up and reachable; and a check on attached storage. It emits scheduled maintenance events when it plans to retire or reboot a host, and it can automatically recover an instance that becomes impaired. We use all of these, and the maintenance events feed one of our own checks. They catch a machine that is down, unreachable, or slated for maintenance, and they stop at the instance level. They confirm the box is up and reachable. They do not verify that each GPU, its on-chip memory, its interconnect, and its network fabric are healthy enough to support distributed training. items.summary: Netflix는 수백 개 GPU로 몇 주간 이어지는 대규모 학습 작업에서 GPU와 네트워크 장비 장애를 사전·실시간으로 감지하고 문제 머신을 사람 개입 없이 자동 복구하는 시스템을 운영한다. 이런 분산 학습은 모든 랭크가 매 스텝 데이터를 주고받는 gang 방식이라 한 참가자만 죽어도 전체 작업이 멈춘다. 클라우드 제공자의 인스턴스 상태 점검은 호스트가 켜져 있고 접근 가능한지만 확인할 뿐, GPU 개별 장치·온칩 메모리·인터커넥트·네트워크 패브릭이 분산 학습을 버틸 만큼 건강한지는 검증하지 못한다. 이 시스템은 Netflix의 Kubernetes 기반 Compute 플랫폼 위에서 학습과 추론 워크로드 모두에 적용된다.
items.why_it_matters: 추천·개인화부터 생성형 AI 기반 추론까지 Netflix 인프라에서 GPU 비중이 가장 빠르게 커지고 비용도 크기 때문에, **가용성과 활용률**을 높이는 것이 곧 동일 작업을 더 적은 비용으로 수행하는 것과 같다. 다중 GPU 분산 학습을 운영하는 조직이라면 장애 허용 설계가 선택이 아닌 필수임을 보여주는 사례다.
items.whats_different: **클라우드 제공자의 기본 인스턴스 상태 점검** 대비, 이 시스템은 GPU 개별 장치·인터커넥트·네트워크 패브릭 수준까지 내려가 건강성을 검증하고 사람 개입 없이 자동 복구한다는 점이 다르다.

items.title: Running Apache Spark experiments in my sleep (and on a plane)
items.abstract: By Prashanth Gedde Narayanaswamy As one of Netflix’s largest and critical data pipelines, member-sessionizer consolidates tens of billions of hourly client events, encompassing user taps, playbacks, and engagement signals, into individual viewing sessions per profile. A quick two-week tuning effort spiraled into two months when standard approaches hit a wall. Because the failures only happened at full production scale, each test took hours, limiting me to just three or four attempts daily. The turning point was changing the goal: instead of trying to speed up a single run, I built a way to run and monitor multiple tests at once and track every result. That mindset led to an unconventional setup: kicking off five Spark jobs at once and monitoring them over spotty inflight Wi-Fi during a day-long trip home, while cloud servers handled the actual heavy lifting. This post covers how I set up that loop, along with the Spark bottlenecks and memory quirks I uncovered along the way. The Scale Dilemma: Small Samples Don’t Catch Scale Bugs Standard engineering wisdom says that you should isolate bugs on small datasets to iterate quickly. That works for standard software bugs, but it fails completely for big data performance bottlenecks. While upgrading our sessionization pipeline from a legacy logging architecture to a modern platform, the new job hit critical failures, including executor Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors, severe shuffle spillage, and thousands of stage retries. None of these issues could be reproduced using sampled data. The failures only triggered at full production scale because of data skew: an idle Netflix tab left streaming overnight generates tens of thousands of telemetry events, while a typical session only produces a handful. A standard 1% sample misses these extreme long-tail sessions entirely. To catch the real bugs, every test run had to execute against a full hour of unsampled production data, along with all the deployment overhead that came with it. The Strategy: Branch-Driven Isolation The biggest win came from a feature in Dataflow , Netflix’s command-line tool for building, testing, and deploying data pipelines. It supports branch-driven development : our workflows run on Maestro ( Netflix’s workflow orchestrator), which schedules and executes the jobs, and they already use a sanitized branch name (the ${dataflow.sanitizedbranch} placeholder). So if I push a branch like pgn/cap-experiment , then the deployed workflow, its tables, and its run namespace all get tagged with that branch name. This eliminates collisions with team members or between my own concurrent runs. With that isolation in place, the model was simple: one branch is one independent experiment . I parameterized the scheduler (cap size, shuffle partitions, heavy-device threshold, feature flags) and gave each variant its own branch and output table. Instead of queuing five sequential tests over 10 hours, I fired off five variants simultaneously against the same time window. Total execution time dropped from the sum of all runs to just the length of the single slowest job. Managing per-branch tables added zero overhead. Dataflow provisions and updates tables automatically from declared schemas without manual DDL. Whenever I modified the event bag structure between experiments, the table schema updated seamlessly, no CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE required. The only real constraint was cluster contention. Because these heavy Spark jobs shared resources with the rest of the company, peak hours sometimes limited me to two concurrent runs instead of five. But even running two or three jobs in parallel was a massive improvement over single-threaded debugging. The key takeaway: don’t focus on making a single multi-hour run faster, build a setup where you can run many experiments simultaneously without them stepping on each other. items.summary: Netflix의 member-sessionizer 파이프라인 튜닝 작업이 샘플 데이터로는 재현 안 되는 **대규모 데이터 스큐** 문제로 2주에서 2개월로 늘어졌다. 원인은 소수 세션이 수만 건의 텔레메트리 이벤트를 생성하는 롱테일 분포로, 1% 샘플링으로는 OOM 에러, 셔플 스필리지, 수천 번의 스테이지 재시도를 잡아낼 수 없었다. 해결책은 단일 실행 속도 개선 대신, Netflix의 Dataflow 도구가 지원하는 브랜치별 자동 격리(sanitized branch name)를 이용해 브랜치마다 독립된 테이블·네임스페이스로 실험을 동시에 여러 개 돌리는 방식이었다. 캡 크기, 셔플 파티션 수 등 파라미터를 바꾼 5개 변형을 동일 시간대에 동시 실행해 총 실행 시간을 전체 합산이 아닌 **가장 느린 작업 하나의 길이**로 줄였다.
items.why_it_matters: 대규모 분산 데이터 파이프라인의 성능 버그는 샘플 데이터로는 재현되지 않는 경우가 많아, 전체 프로덕션 규모 테스트와 병렬 실험 인프라가 실질적인 디버깅 속도를 좌우한다는 교훈을 준다.
items.whats_different: 순차적으로 단일 실행을 최적화하던 기존 방식 대신, 브랜치마다 테이블·네임스페이스를 자동 격리해 여러 실험을 동시에 충돌 없이 실행하는 접근으로 전환했다.

items.title: Jeva: System One Models from First Principles
items.abstract: System one models enable direct, low-latency decision-making. Yet recent practice of predicting an answer from serialized text does not, by itself, respect the structure of a decision problem. We argue that current designs underemphasize four important structural requirements. (i) null-aware: Models should distinguish answer absence from uncertainty among candidates; (ii) permutation-invariant: Reordering alternatives should not change the decision; (iii) option-scalable: Growing candidate sets should not require redefining the output space; (iv) cacheable: Request-independent computation over recurring alternatives should be reusable across requests. We introduce Jeva, a decision-native architecture that addresses these requirements jointly. A shared encoder independently represents the request and each option, while a compact decision stack refines only the request state against immutable option memory. Symmetric aggregation yields permutation-equivariant probabilities; shared scoring accommodates variable-size candidate sets. A separate coverage estimate distinguishes answer absence from candidate competition, enabling explicit null outcomes. Request-independent option representations and layer projections support reuse across newly assembled sets. These mechanisms unify Choice, Noul, and Score outputs. Across evaluations, Jeva combines strong typed-decision performance with near-perfect null detection and no decision flips under any tested permutations. It scales to thousands of candidates and substantially reduces latency through cross-request reuse without changing decisions.
items.title_ko: Jeva 공개 — 순서 바꿔도 결정 불변, 수천 개 후보로 확장되는 '의사결정 전용' 시스템원 모델
items.summary: 이 논문은 텍스트 직렬화 후 답을 예측하는 기존 시스템원 모델 설계가 결정 문제의 구조를 제대로 반영하지 못한다고 지적한다. 저자들은 **null-aware, 순열 불변, 옵션 확장성, 캐시 가능성** 네 가지 구조적 요건을 제시하고, 이를 동시에 만족하는 결정 전용 아키텍처 Jeva를 제안한다. Jeva는 요청과 각 옵션을 독립적으로 표현하는 공유 인코더와, 고정된 옵션 메모리에 대해 요청 상태만 정제하는 결정 스택으로 구성되며, 대칭 집계로 순열 등변 확률을 산출하고 커버리지 추정으로 답 부재와 후보 간 경쟁을 구분한다. 평가 결과 Jeva는 강력한 유형별 결정 성능과 거의 완벽한 null 탐지, 테스트된 모든 순열에서 결정 변화 없음을 보였고, **수천 개 후보로 확장되면서도** 요청 간 재사용을 통해 지연시간을 크게 줄였다.
items.why_it_matters: 표 형태나 후보 선택형 의사결정 문제에서 순서나 후보 수 변화에 민감한 기존 모델의 신뢰성 문제를 구조적으로 해결하려는 시도로, 실시간 추천·검색·분류 시스템 설계에 시사점을 준다.
items.whats_different: 기존의 텍스트 직렬화 기반 답 예측 방식 대비, 요청과 옵션 표현을 분리하고 재사용 가능한 옵션 메모리를 두어 순열 불변성과 대규모 후보 확장성을 동시에 확보한 점이 다르다.

items.title: Does Stacking Beat Your Best Model?
items.abstract: It only helps when your models make different mistakes. The post Does Stacking Beat Your Best Model? appeared first on Towards Data Science .
items.title_ko: 스태킹 앙상블, 언제 단일 최강 모델을 이길까 — 핵심은 '서로 다른 오류 패턴'
items.summary: 이 글은 스태킹(stacking) 앙상블이 항상 최고 성능의 단일 모델을 능가하는 것은 아니라는 점을 다룬다. 스태킹이 실제로 도움이 되는 경우는 모델들이 **서로 다른 종류의 실수**를 할 때뿐이라는 것이 핵심 주장이다. 즉 모델들의 예측 오류가 유사하다면 스태킹으로 결합해도 성능 향상 효과가 크지 않다.
items.why_it_matters: 실무에서 여러 모델을 무작정 쌓기보다, 모델 간 오류의 다양성을 먼저 점검해야 불필요한 복잡도 증가 없이 성능 개선을 얻을 수 있다.
